rule.name: AWS_Credentials_Leak
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker could find the leaked credentials, enabling access to accounts, services, and confidential data. 

Cause

How does it happen

AWS credentials are written to a file, database, or exposed in a web context. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When using AWS credentials, they should only be read from a safe place and never written or accessed within the code. The credentials should be used for the needed purpose and nothing else, for example, to use the AWS SDK. 

]]

rule.name: DynamoDB_NoSQL_Injection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

NoSQL Injections may result in unexpected behavior and may allow an attacker to modify, retrieve or delete arbitrary documents within the database, thus allowing them to bypass logic checks and privileges and more. 

Cause

How does it happen

DynamoDB is a key-value pairs-based database that is classified as a NoSQL database (provided by AWS).To interact with DynamoDB, one can use an SQL-Compatible language, called PartiQL. When tainted data is naively concatenated within the PartiQL query, the application is subject to NoSQL injection. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always use the built-in parameterization of PartiQL when constructing the queries. 

]]

rule.name: Hardcoded_AWS_Credentials
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Hardcoded credentials expose the application to credential leakage. If an attacker gains access to the source code, they will be able to steal the embedded passwords, and use them to impersonate a valid user, compromising any access, data and functionality this account has with AWS. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application codebase contains AWS credentials as string literals embedded in the source code. This hardcoded value is then passed as credentials to an AWS client. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not hardcode any secret data in source code, especially not credentials of any kind.  
    • In particular, user passwords should be stored in a database or directory service, and protected with a strong password hash (e.g. bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2, or Argon2). 

]]

rule.name: Permission_Manipulation_In_S3
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If an attacker is able to determine read or write permissions to a specific object in S3, they may use it to grant unexpected permissions. Such permissions may allow: 
* Providing access to themselves to read sensitive information* Providing access to overwrite certain objects, resulting in loss of data or denial of service 

Cause

How does it happen

How to avoid it

    • Do not rely on user input to determine access control for S3 objects.

rule.name: Race_Condition_Global_Scope
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

In AWS Lambda, leaks across invocations can occur in the same execution environment, due to this problem. 
A race condition can cause erratic or unexpected application behaviour. Additionally, if a race condition can be influenced directly by users, an attacker may choose to replay a race condition until they obtain a desired result, allowing them to induce certain application behaviour that is not part of its intentional design. 

Cause

How does it happen

The serverless function environment relies on a global context to increase performance, where initializations and libraries loads are executed at the function "Cold Start". These initialization are shared across different executions. Within a serverless context where a single instance may handle multiple requests without being destroyed, the usage of global variables in function logic may lead to unexpected behaviours. 
For example, if a global variable is used to hold a user identifier, and this identifier does not change across executions, an attacker may be able to control the function flow to his advantage. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When dealing with static member variables - always consider that these are shared across all instances of an object 
    • Do not rely on global variables 

]]

rule.name: Unrestricted_Delete_S3
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If an attacker is allowed to determine what object/bucket is deleted from the S3 instance, they may delete arbitrary objects/buckets that were not intended to be available to users, and in case there are no backups cause availability and integrity issues. If the application logic relies on this data as well, may lead to unexpected behavior. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application's code directly relies on unvalidated user-supplied inputs as a key for deleting an object or bucket from S3. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not rely on user inputs as literal keys for deleting an object or bucket in S3. 
    • If dynamic deletion is required on a per-user basis, store these keys in a container associated with the user, such as session variables or a database, and use them as required. Ensure such keys cannot be altered by the user. 

]]

rule.name: Unrestricted_Read_S3
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If an attacker is allowed to determine what object is retrieved from the S3 instance and returned to them, they may retrieve arbitrary objects that were not intended to be available to users, disclosing potentially sensitive contents. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application's code directly relies on unvalidated user-supplied inputs as a key for retrieving and object from S3, whose contents are later returned to the user. If this S3 instance contains sensitive information, an attacker could provide a key to retrieve other objects that may contain other users' information or sensitive information not intended for external user consumption. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not rely on user inputs as literal keys for retrieval of S3 objects. 
    • If dynamic retrieval is required on a per-user basis, store these keys in a container associated with the user, such as session variables or a database, and use them as required. Ensure such keys cannot be altered by the user. 

]]

rule.name: Unrestricted_Write_S3
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If an attacker can choose where to write to in an S3 instance, they may overwrite existing objects with arbitrary ones resulting in loss of data, or, if this data is relied upon by the application, unexpected behavior and denial of service. 

Cause

How does it happen

If user inputs dictate where content is written into in an S3 instance, then they may also choose from existing objects, thus overwriting them. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not rely on user inputs as literal keys for determining a write location of S3 objects. 
    • If dynamic writing to different locations is required on a per-user basis, generate and store these keys in a container associated with the user, such as session variables or a database, and use them as required. Ensure such keys cannot be altered by the user, so that they may not arbitrarily overwrite data. 

]]

rule.name: Use_of_Hardcoded_Cryptographic_Key_On_Server
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Static, unchangeable encryption keys in the source code can be stolen by an attacker with access to the source code or the application binaries. Once the attacker has the encryption key, this can be used to gain access to any encrypted secret data, thus violating the confidentiality of the data. Furthermore, it would be impossible to replace the encryption key once stolen. Note that if this is a product that can be installed numerous times, the encryption key will always be the same, allowing an attacker to break all instances at the same cost. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application code uses an encryption key to encrypt and decrypt sensitive data. While it is important to create this encryption key randomly and keep it secret, the application has a single, static key embedded in plain text in the source code.  
An attacker could gain access to the source code - whether in the source control system, developer workstations, or the server filesystem or product binaries themselves. Once the attacker has gained access to the source code, it is trivial to retrieve the plain text encryption key and use it to decrypt the sensitive data that the application was protecting. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Generic Guidance: 
    • Do not store any sensitive information, such as encryption keys, in plain text. 
    • Never hardcode encryption keys in the application source code.  
    • Implement proper key management, including dynamically generating random keys, protecting keys, and replacing keys as necessary.  
    • Specific Recommendations: 
    • Remove the hardcoded encryption key from the application source code. Instead, retrieve the key from an external, protected store. 

]]

rule.name: User_Based_SDK_Configurations
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If the configurations are different from what the developer expected, at best, inconsistent behavior will occur. Additionally, the availability and integrity of the app may be damaged. 

Cause

How does it happen

A malicious actor might be able to change the configuration of the AWS-SDK used by the lambda. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Don't embed user input inside AWS SDK configuration 
    • If it's necessary, make sure you validate the values against a whitelist. 

]]

rule.name: Outdated_Encryption_Algorithm
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

While outdated encryption algorithms or their parameters are not a risk per se as they have not yet been deemed broken, deprecated or obsolete - they are still considered outdated, and may face obsolescence in the near future. Weak encryption which is almost feasible to decrypt using cryptanalysis and brute force attacks will most likely be decryptable in the near future, exposing its contents to a persistent enough attacker. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses an encryption algorithm or its parameters that are considered outdated, and may become a liability in the future. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When developing new software - always use futureproof encryption algorithms with futureproof parameters 
    • For legacy code - consider a planned migration away from outdated encryption algorithms to stay ahead of their obsolescence 
    • Keep up-to-date with FIPS-approved and NIST-recommended encryption algorithms and their parameters 
    • Always ensure to properly configure encryption, such as by securely generating encryption keys, securely randomizing IVs, and using modern and trusted ciphers 

]]

rule.name: Outdated_Hashing_Function
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

While outdated hashing functions are not a risk per-se as they have no yet been deemed broken, deprecated or obsolete - they are still considered outdated, and may face obsolescence in the near future. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses a hashing function that is considered outdated, and may become a liability in the future. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When developing new software - always use futureproof hashing functions 
    • For legacy code - consider a planned migration away from outdated hashing functions, to stay ahead of their obsolescence 
    • Keep up-to-date with FIPS-approved and NIST-recommended hashing functions 
    • Always ensure to properly configure cost-based hashing functions with values that meet industry based practices 

]]

rule.name: Arbitrary_File_Write
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Unvalidated malicious files, which can be written to arbitrary paths on the file system, could pose various risks based on implementation and underlying technologies:- An attacker could attack the server by uploading a malicious code file and executing it on the server- An uploaded file could overwrite critical server files such as configurations or data- An uploaded malicious file could be served to other users, allowing attackers to abuse the application as a watering hole to attack the rest of the userbase 

Cause

How does it happen

The application fails to validate a filename before saving it to the filesystem, which could allow attackers to modify the directory where the uploaded files are saved to; an attacker could potentially break out of the upload directory and write the file to an arbitrary location on the file system, overwrite other files in the file system, and upload files with potentially dangerous file extensions. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Storage: If possible, avoid saving uploaded files to disk on the server; instead storing them in external data storage, e.g., database or document management system. 
    • Location: User files should be stored in an isolated directory, outside of the web site's directory with direct browsing disabled. When required, the application should explicitly read the file in code and stream the contents to the user applicatively. 
    • Assurance of non-execution: Files uploaded from users should be explicitly marked as non-executable by the web / application server, e.g., in a configuration file or by directory. 
    • Validation: Always validate all user input. In particular, enforce an allow-list of allowed file types, according to the file extension and/or MIME type. Do not allow arbitrary files (such as .ASP, .PHP, .JSP, .EXE, .HTML, and so on). For example, accept only images such as .GIF, .JPG, .PNG, .BMP; these lists should be based on business requirements. If business requirements include non-media files such as documents, executables or code - consider adding another layer of security which would scan these files for malicious content. 
    • Renaming: Explicitly impose a pre-defined extension according to the file type before saving the file to disk. This can be a hardcoded extension or a configured list of allowed file types. 
    • Privileges: As a measure of Defense-in-Depth, configure the application server to execute in a limited system account with minimal OS privileges.  

]]

rule.name: CGI_Stored_XSS
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The attacker could use legitimate access to the application to submit modified data, which would be saved by the application to some data-store. This stored data would then be used to dynamically generate output to a generic output writer - in some scenarios, such as with CGI scripts, this output will be sent directly to the user's browser, which would trigger the attack. 
A successful XSS exploit would allow an attacker to rewrite web pages and insert malicious scripts which would alter the intended output. This could include HTML fragments, CSS styling rules, arbitrary JavaScript, or references to third party code. An attacker could use this to steal users' passwords, collect personal data such as credit card details, provide false information, or run malware. From the victim’s point of view, this is performed by the genuine website, and the victim would blame the site for incurred damage. 

Cause

How does it happen

In order to exploit this vulnerability, an attacker would load the malicious payload into some data-store, typically via regular forms on other web pages. Afterwards, the application reads this data from the data-store, and embeds it within the web page as displayed for another user. 
The application creates web pages that include untrusted data, whether from user input, the application’s database, or from other external sources. The untrusted data is embedded directly in the page's HTML, causing the browser to display it as part of the web page. If the input includes HTML fragments or JavaScript, these are displayed too, and the user cannot tell that this is not the intended page. The vulnerability is the result of directly embedding arbitrary data without first encoding it in a format that would prevent the browser from treating it like HTML or code instead of plain text. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Fully encode all dynamic data, regardless of source, before embedding it in output. 
    • Encoding should be context-sensitive. For example: 
    • HTML encoding for HTML content 
    • HTML Attribute encoding for data output to attribute values 
    • JavaScript encoding for server-generated JavaScript 
    • It is recommended to use the platform-provided encoding functionality, or known security libraries for encoding output. 
    • Implement a Content Security Policy (CSP) with explicit whitelists for the application's resources only.  
    • As an extra layer of protection, validate all untrusted data, regardless of source (note this is not a replacement for encoding). Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • In the Content-Type HTTP response header, explicitly define character encoding (charset) for the entire page.  
    • Set the HTTPOnly flag on the session cookie for "Defense in Depth", to prevent any successful XSS exploits from stealing the cookie. 

]]

rule.name: Command_Injection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker could run arbitrary system-level OS commands on the application server host. Depending on the application’s OS permissions, these could include: 
* File actions (read / create / modify / delete)* Open a network connection to the attacker’s server* Start and stop system services* Modify the running application* Complete server takeover 

Cause

How does it happen

In this case, the application receives data from the user input, and passes it as a string to the Operating System. This unvalidated data is then executed by the OS as a system command, running with the same system privileges as the application. 
The application runs an OS system-level command to complete it's task, rather than via the application code. The command includes untrusted data, that may be controllable by an attacker. This untrusted string may contain malicious system-level commands engineered by an attacker, which could be executed as though the attacker were running commands directly on the application server. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Refactor the code to avoid any direct shell command execution. Instead, use platform provided APIs or library calls. 
    • If it is impossible to remove the command execution, execute only static commands that do not include dynamic, user-controlled data. 
    • Validate all input, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified format, rather than rejecting bad patterns (blacklist). Parameters should be limited to an allowed character set, and non-validated input should be dropped. In addition to characters, check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • In order to minimize damage as a measure of defense in depth, configure the application to run using a restricted user account that has no unnecessary OS privileges. 
    • If possible, isolate all OS commands to use a separate dedicated user account that has minimal privileges only for the specific commands and files used by the application, according to the Principle of Least Privilege. 

]]

rule.name: NoSQL_Injection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

NoSQL databases are designed to store and retrieve data flexibly, schema-less, often using key-value pairs, document-oriented structures, or graph databases. If a query conducted on a NoSQL database contains user-supplied input without proper sanitization and validation, an attacker can manipulate the query to inject arbitrary values, logic, or code. 
An attacker able to modify the syntax of a raw NoSQL query could inject malicious scripts or commands, such as an infinite loop (while(1)), leading to a Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack by consuming server resources. They might also inject a return statement to alter the query results, causing the application to return unauthorized or incorrect data. 
Broadly, NoSQL injections may result in unexpected behavior and allow an attacker to modify, retrieve, or delete arbitrary documents within the database. This can lead to bypassing application logic, security checks, and access controls. For instance, attackers could escalate privileges, access sensitive information, access all of the system's data, or disrupt application functionality before launching a DoS attack. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses tainted values from an untrusted source to craft a raw query. This allows the attacker to modify the syntax of the query, injecting new syntax, thus resulting in a NoSQL Injection. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Validate all untrusted data, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure rather than rejecting bad patterns. 
    • In particular, check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values. 
    • Restrict access to database objects and functionality, according to the Principle of Least Privilege. 
    • Do not use dynamically concatenated strings to construct NoSQL filters. 
    • Instead of unsafe string concatenation, use secure database components such as parameterized queries and object bindings (for example, commands and parameters). 
    • Never use potentially tainted inputs when crafting raw queries 
    • Always use a Document-Object Mapper to perform CRUD actions. A Document-Object Mapper ensures objects are paired to documents and, under the hood, performs proper sanitization of values to ensure no tainted values ever alter the syntax of queries. Document-object mappers are used very similarly to SQL's ORMs by mapping data to objects and vice versa. 

]]

rule.name: SQL_Injection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker could directly access all of the system's data. The attacker would likely be able to steal any sensitive information stored by the system, including private user information, credit card details, proprietary business data, and any other secret data. Likewise, the attacker could possibly modify or erase existing data, or even add new bogus data. In some scenarios, it may even be possible to execute code on the database.  
In addition to disclosing or altering confidential information directly, this vulnerability might also be used to achieve secondary effects, such as bypassing authentication, subverting security checks, or forging a data trail.  
Further increasing the likelihood of exploit is the fact that this flaw is easy for attackers to find, and easy to exploit. 

Cause

How does it happen

Note that an attacker can exploit this vulnerability either by modifying the URL, or by submitting malicious data in the user input or other request fields. 
The application stores and manages data in a database, by submitting a textual SQL query to the database engine for processing. The application creates the query by simple string concatenation, embedding untrusted data. However, there is no separation between data and code; furthermore, the embedded data is neither checked for data type validity nor subsequently sanitized. Thus, the untrusted data could contain SQL commands, or modify the intended query. The database would interpret the altered query and commands as if they originated from the application, and execute them accordingly. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Validate all untrusted data, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns.  
    • In particular, check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values. 
    • Restrict access to database objects and functionality, according to the Principle of Least Privilege. 
    • Do not use dynamically concatenate strings to construct SQL queries.  
    • Prefer using DB Stored Procedures for all data access, instead of ad-hoc dynamic queries.  
    • Instead of unsafe string concatenation, use secure database components such as parameterized queries and object bindings (for example, commands and parameters).  
    • Alternatively, an even better solution is to use an ORM library, in order to pre-define and encapsulate the allowed commands enabled for the application, instead of dynamically accessing the database directly. In this way the code plane and data plane should be isolated from each other. 

]]

rule.name: Server_Side_Template_Injection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

What might happen

Cause

How does it happen

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

rule.name: Absolute_Path_Traversal
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker could define arbitrary file path for the application to use, potentially leading to: 
* Stealing sensitive files, such as configuration or system files* Overwriting files such as program binaries, configuration files, or system files* Deleting critical files, causing denial of service (DoS). 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses user input in the file path for accessing files on the application server’s local disk. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • 1. Ideally, avoid depending on dynamic data for file selection. 
    • 2. Validate all input, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values

Risk

What might happen

The attacker could use legitimate access to the application to submit modified data, which would be returned as output without proper sanitization. This would then be used to dynamically generate output to a generic output writer - in some scenarios, such as with CGI scripts, this output is sent directly to the user's browser, which would trigger the attack. 
A successful XSS exploit would allow an attacker to rewrite web pages and insert malicious scripts which would alter the intended output. This could include HTML fragments, CSS styling rules, arbitrary JavaScript, or references to third party code. An attacker could use this to steal users' passwords, collect personal data such as credit card details, provide false information, or run malware. From the victim’s point of view, this is performed by the genuine website, and the victim would blame the site for incurred damage. 

Cause

How does it happen

Note that an attacker can exploit this vulnerability either by modifying the URL, or by submitting malicious data in the user input or other request fields. 
The application creates web pages that include untrusted data, whether from user input, the application’s database, or from other external sources. The untrusted data is embedded directly in the page's HTML, causing the browser to display it as part of the web page. If the input includes HTML fragments or JavaScript, these are displayed too, and the user cannot tell that this is not the intended page. The vulnerability is the result of directly embedding arbitrary data without first encoding it in a format that would prevent the browser from treating it like HTML or code instead of plain text. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Fully encode all dynamic data, regardless of source, before embedding it in output. 
    • Encoding should be context-sensitive. For example: 
    • HTML encoding for HTML content 
    • HTML Attribute encoding for data output to attribute values 
    • JavaScript encoding for server-generated JavaScript 
    • It is recommended to use the platform-provided encoding functionality, or known security libraries for encoding output. 
    • Implement a Content Security Policy (CSP) with explicit whitelists for the application's resources only.  
    • As an extra layer of protection, validate all untrusted data, regardless of source (note this is not a replacement for encoding). Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • In the Content-Type HTTP response header, explicitly define character encoding (charset) for the entire page.  
    • Set the HTTPOnly flag on the session cookie for "Defense in Depth", to prevent any successful XSS exploits from stealing the cookie. 

]]

rule.name: Connection_String_Injection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If an attacker could manipulate the application’s connection string to the database server, they might be able do any of the following: 
* Damage application performance (by increasing the MIN POOL SIZE)* Tamper with the network connection (for example, via TRUSTED CONNECTION)* Direct the application to the attacker’s bogus database* Discover the password to the system account on the database (by a brute-force attack). 

Cause

How does it happen

In order to communicate with the database, or with another external server (for example, Active Directory), the application dynamically constructs a connection string. This connection string includes untrusted data, which may be controlled by a malicious user. Since it is not constrained or properly sanitized, the untrusted data could be used to maliciously manipulate the connection string. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Validate all input, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • Do not allow users to control the database connection string. Avoid dynamically building connection strings based on untrusted data, especially user input. 
    • Store all connection strings in appropriate configuration mechanisms. If it is necessary to dynamically construct a connection string at runtime, do not include untrusted data directly in the connection string; instead, allow users to select from pre-defined connection strings. 

]]

rule.name: Dangerous_File_Inclusion
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If an attacker can select the name of the library, or the location of the code file that is loaded by the application, they would be able to cause the application to execute arbitrary code. This effectively allows the attacker to control the code run by the application. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses untrusted data to specify the library or code file, without proper sanitization. This causes the application to load any arbitrary code, as specified. The loaded code will then be executed. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not dynamically load code libraries, especially not based on user input. 
    • If it is necessary to use untrusted data to select the library to be loaded, verify the selected library name matches a predefined set of whitelisted library names. Alternatively, use the value as an identifier to select from the whitelisted libraries. 
    • Validate any untrusted data used to load or process libraries or code files by performing an integrity check on the requested resource. 

]]

rule.name: Deserialization_of_Untrusted_Data
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker that can modify serialized object data, might be able to control the loading and execution of the object code. This could allow the attacker to alter internal object state; consume arbitrary amounts of data-based resources, effectively causing a DoS (Denial of Service); bypass data validation, thus exploiting follow-on vulnerabilities; and possibly even execute arbitrary code on the server. 

Cause

How does it happen

Applications often need to output object data into a serialized format, in order to persist to disk or stream over the network. The application is then required to deserialize the binary data, and convert it back into internal object data. 
However, no validation is done on the binary input, and the untrusted data is loaded directly into arbitrary internal objects. Furthermore, the deserialization process often executes custom code based on the input data. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • If possible, prefer to avoid deserializing untrusted data in your code.  
    • Where applicable, consider marking object fields as transient, to prevent them from being deserialized.  
    • Implement custom deserialization, and explicitly validate all loaded data and create a new object, instead of just deserializing the object directly. 
    • Override the ObjectInputStream.resolveClass() method to whitelist deserializable classes, and prevent arbitrary classes from being loaded.  
    • Classes that should not ever be deserialized, yet inherit from a Serializable class, can explicitly declare a final readObject() method, which always throws an exception to prevent loading objects of this class via deserialization.  
    • Consider using digital signatures or HMAC to enforce signature verification and allow deserialization only with an authenticated digital signature. 
    • If the application includes the commons-collections library, either remove this library if it is not required, otherwise manually patch the JAR file to remove the "InvokerTransformer" class (and thoroughly test that this does not break the application). 

]]

rule.name: JWT_No_Signature_Verification
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If the JWT signature is not validated, there is no way to guarantee the integrity of the data present in the JWT body. A malicious user could then add their own claims and potentially have access to other users' accounts or protected resources. 

Cause

How does it happen

During the JWT verification step, the application does not validate the JWT signature and only decodes/parses its claims. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Make sure to use the appropriate method for JWT verification, which guarantees the signature is valid. 
    • Make sure that the verification step includes not only the signature check but also the verification of the expiration date and all the content relevant to your application requirements. 

]]

rule.name: LDAP_Injection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker that is able to alter the application’s LDAP query with arbitrary data would have control over the results returned from the User Directory server. Most commonly, this would enable an attacker to bypass authentication, or impersonate another user.   
Furthermore, this flaw can have various additional effects, depending on the architecture and usage model of the Directory service. Depending on how the application is using LDAP, the attacker could potentially do any of the following: 
* Bypass authentication* Impersonate another user* Subvert authorization* Escalate privileges* Modify user attributes and group membership* Access sensitive data 

Cause

How does it happen

The application communicates with an LDAP server, such as Active Directory, by sending a textual LDAP query or command. The application creates the query by simply concatenating strings, including untrusted data that may be controlled by an attacker. Since the data is neither validated nor properly sanitized, the input could contain LDAP commands that would be interpreted as such by the LDAP server. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Validate all external data, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist. Accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. 
    • Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • Avoid creating LDAP queries that are directly dependent on untrusted external data, if possible. For example, retrieve the user object from the LDAP server, and examine it's attributes in application code. 

]]

rule.name: Observable_Timing_Discrepancy
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Using an insecure form of credential storage could expose users' and/or administrators' credentials to brute-force, rainbow-table, and other types of attacks. Even if the application uses a secure credential storage mechanism, it's still possible to implement the solution in an insecure manner and reduce the security of the stored credentials. 
Using a non-constant-time comparison between hashes or passwords may cause side-channel data leakage. A sophisticated attacker may be able to retrieve the challenge string by building a statistical model of the timing differences between carefully chosen authentication attempts. 

Cause

How does it happen

Regular comparison operations are usually optimized for performance. When these comparison methods operate over strings, they iterate each character on the two strings. If they find a difference, they immediately stop and return a false result for the comparison. The problem with this is the unintended side-channel vector available to an attacker who can control one of the comparison terms. Let's assume the challenge to break is "AAA". An attacker may send "BAA" and later send "ABA", noticing a slight increase in the average time taken to return the comparison result simply because the comparison loop over each character on the strings now performs two iterations instead of only one (failing on the first character). 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Using constant time comparison functions is crucial while validating hashes and MACs to ensure timing does allow deriving any information regarding compared values. There are several secure options available: 
    • JCA MessageDigest isEqual() method 
    • BouncyCastle Strings and Arrays utils classes constantTimeAreEqual() method 
    • SpringSecurity PasswordEncoder matches() method 

]]

rule.name: Plain_Text_Transport_Layer_in_Server
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Sending data over the network is inherently risky, unless the communication channel is protected using a secured protocol. This is especially true for mobile devices that are often connected to non-secure networks and untrusted hotspots. An attacker can easily eavesdrop on the information being sent over the air and retrieve it. In certain cases, an attacker may even manipulate the data to attack users and servers - for example, by injecting a forged, malicious login page into a legitimate website. 

Cause

How does it happen

The app starts a server that listens for connections using an insecure protocol like HTTP, which will cause the underlying channel to use cleartext communications, without securing it with SSL/TLS. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always use a secure protocol to send and receive sensitive data. Always choose the use of SSL/TLS over a plain-text connection, like HTTPS instead of HTTP. 

]]

rule.name: Relative_Path_Traversal
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker could define arbitrary file path for the application to use, potentially leading to: 
* Stealing sensitive files, such as configuration or system files* Overwriting files such as program binaries, configuration files, or system files* Deleting critical files, causing denial of service (DoS). 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses user input in the file path for accessing files on the application server’s local disk. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • 1. Ideally, avoid depending on dynamic data for file selection. 
    • 2. Validate all input, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • 4. Accept dynamic data only for the filename, not for the path and folders. 
    • 5. Ensure that file path is fully canonicalized. 
    • 6. Explicitly limit the application to use a designated folder that is separate from the applications binary folder. 
    • 7. Restrict the privileges of the application’s OS user to necessary files and folders. The application should not be able to write to the application binary folder, and should not read anything outside of the application folder and data folder. 

]]

rule.name: SSRF
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker can abuse this flaw to make arbitrary requests, originating from the application server. This can be exploited to scan internal services; proxy attacks into a protected network; bypass network controls; download unauthorized files; access internal services and management interfaces; and possibly control the contents of requests and even steal server credentials. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application accepts a URL (or other data) from the user, and uses this to make a request to another remote server. 
However, the attacker can inject an arbitrary URL into the request, causing the application to connect to any server the attacker wants. Thus, the attacker can abuse the application to gain access to services that would not otherwise be accessable, and cause the request to ostensibly originate from the application server. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not connect to arbitrary services based on user input. 
    • If possible, the application should have the user's browser retrieve the desired information directly.  
    • If it is necessary for the application to proxy the request on the server, explicitly whitelist the allowed target URLs, and do not include any sensitive server information. 

]]

rule.name: Sensitive_Information_Exposure_in_Cleartext_Channel
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Sensitive and personal details, such as passwords, social security numbers, credit card data, and other forms of PII (Personally Identifiable Information), must always be protected when being transmitted over the network. Sending this private data over an unencrypted channel, such as without using SSL/TLS or other form of encryption, can reveal the users' secret information and expose them to risks of impersonation, identity theft, and financial fraud.  
If the SSL/TLS channel is terminated on a front-end webserver, reverse proxy, or the like, this issue can be ignored. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application handles sensitive and private information in several ways. At a certain point, this secret data is sent over the network, however the application does not use SSL/TLS, or any other secure protocol, and does not ensure the data is encrypted before sending it over the unprotected channel. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always use http.ServeTLS or http.ListenAndServeTLS to ensure the communication channel uses TLS. 
    • Always protect all PII and other sensitive data, especially when it is being sent over the network.  
    • Use SSL/TLS whenever transmitting sensitive data. Alternatively, other encrypted protocols, such as IPsec or SSH, can also be used.  
    • Reconsider if the application absolutely requires these personal details. Data that is not received cannot be exposed.  
    • In web applications, do not output personal info directly to the response without verifying the channel is secured. 

]]

rule.name: Unsafe_Archive_Unpacking
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Extracting files from an untrusted archive using libraries or methods that do not validate file names could allow attackers to manipulate the extraction process to write files in arbitrary locations. Depending on execution privileges, this may allow overwriting certain files which would allow attackers further access to the system - at worst, an attacker can overwrite files that would lead to a complete system takeover. 

Cause

How does it happen

Archive files are used to contain and often compress multiple files and folders. File names within the archive should contain a file's relative path, for when the archive is extracted - this allows the extracted archive to retain its original file and directory structure. However the affected code does not properly validate the archived file's filename to ensure it is a well-formed relative normalized path without traversal.To ensure no traversal is allowed in code, unarchiving should validate a file name is not an absolute path (e.g. starts with /, rather than c:\ or ~/) or a relative path with path traversal symbols such as ../ or ..\. Failure to validate the extraction path could allow the unarchiving process to write files outside of the designated extraction destination, by navigating out of the target directory and writing an arbitrary file to an arbitrary location, often overwriting existing files.This vulnerability is also known as an "evilarc" or "ZipSlip" vulnerability. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When implementing proprietary unarchiving code - always validate file paths by normalizing them to remove any traversal symbols 
    • Consider using existing unarchiving libraries that do validate or normalize file paths on extraction 

]]

rule.name: Unsafe_Reflection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Using reflections in Go along with the unsafe package may allow attackers to invoke completely arbitrary code of their choice. 
Reflections directly affected by user input may, at best, result in unexpected or unstable behavior. At worst, it may allow attackers to inject and execute malicious code, invoke unexpected methods or classes from within the code to bypass logic flow or manipulate data and more. 

Cause

How does it happen

Reflections are a method of coding wherein classes, methods or built-in functions are programmatically invoked by their name. If this name is dynamically determined from user inputs, then these inputs may change the flow of code, invoke unexpected or unintended code and, at times, allow injection of new, malicious code. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid using any form of dynamic code evaluation, and specifically, avoid using reflections unless absolutely required. 
    • If dynamic evaluation is not required, use logic flow to determine which functions to run 
    • If dynamic evaluation is required, enforce a white-list of allowed code segments to ensure arbitrary code cannot be executed 

]]

rule.name: Insecure_Credential_Storage_Mechanism
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

 Not using a standardized, publicly known solution for credential storage that has been under scrutiny by the security researcher community, will reduce the security of the credential storage used to access the application. 
Using an insecure form of credential storage could expose users' and/or administrators' credentials to brute-force, rainbow-table and other types of attacks. 

Cause

How does it happen

 The application is not storing credentials via a known secure mechanism. 
The method used to store the credentials is insecure. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Other means of credential storage are unsafe to use because they have either not been subject to cryptanalysis by security researchers or they have been broken or weakened. 
    • Credential storage, namely passwords, should be carefully done by using a password hashing function. Most hashing functions have been created with speed as a pre-requisite, to create cryptographically secure hashes for file integrity and other purposes, making them ill fit for direct use with passwords; other functions have been broken in the past due to collisions or other security problems (MD5, SHA-1, etc...) . 
    • Our recommendations for secure credential storage functions include: 
    • Argon2 
    • scrypt 
    • bcrypt 
    • PBKDF2 (for legacy compatibility only) 

]]

rule.name: Insecure_Scrypt_Parameters
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Although scrypt has been designed specifically to thwart brute-force and other fast attacks, having the wrong input parameters defined may result in significant weakening of the algorithm's output. 
Modern hash functions usually have a cost (or similar) parameter the user can set to determine how much computational power should be used in hashing the password. A higher value means a slower computation, but also makes it slower to attack, as each attempt will take longer to perform. 

Cause

How does it happen

The parameters N, r and p are not set with secure values. 
Setting too low a cost value may significantly reduce the security of the password hash. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • In scrypt, these parameters are N, r and p. N defines the CPU/memory cost parameter, r defines the blocksize parameter, and p is the parallelization parameter. N and r define how hard it is to perform one attempt, and p defines how many processors should be used to perform the calculation. The currently defined set of values determined as secure are N >= 2^15, r >= 8 and p >= 2. 
    • Choosing an appropriate cost parameter depends on the underlying hashing algorithm in place and what the purpose of the key derivation function is. The most common purpose is authenticating interactive logins, so the threshold values on the cost parameters for this query have been set accordingly. 

]]

rule.name: Insufficient_Bcrypt_Cost
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Setting the bcrypt cost parameter with too low a value will result in significant reduction of the resulting hash's security. 
Modern hash functions usually have a cost (or similar) parameter the user can set to determine how much computational power should be used in hashing the password. A higher value means a slower computation, but also makes it slower to attack, as each attempt will take longer to perform. 

Cause

How does it happen

The cost parameter for the bcrypt function is too low. 
Setting too low a cost value may significantly reduce the security of the password hash. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Bcrypt's cost parameter should be set at the default value (10) or higher. Reducing this number will reduce the computational effort required for computing hash from the password, weakening the resulting hash, making it easier for an attacker to crack it. 
    • Choosing an appropriate cost parameter depends on the underlying hashing algorithm in place and what the purpose of the key derivation function is. The most common purpose is authenticating interactive logins, so the threshold values on the cost parameters for this query have been set accordingly. 

]]

rule.name: Insufficient_Output_Length
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

In this instance, the key derivation function's output length is too low. This can cause collisions where different passwords will hash to the same value, causing successful authentication where it should not happen. 
Modern hash functions usually have a cost (or similar) parameter the user can set to determine how much computational power should be used in hashing the password. A higher value means a slower computation, but also makes it slower to attack, as each attempt will take longer to perform. 

Cause

How does it happen

The output length of the key derivation function is too low. 
Setting too low a cost value may significantly reduce the security of the password hash. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Using these functions, however, is not enough to guarantee a secure credential storage mechanism. In order to avoid collisions, the safe length of the key derivation function's output should be 32 bytes or higher. 
    • Choosing an appropriate cost parameter depends on the underlying hashing algorithm in place and what the purpose of the key derivation function is. The most common purpose is authenticating interactive logins, so the threshold values on the cost parameters for this query have been set accordingly. 

]]

rule.name: PBKDF2_Insufficient_Iteration_Count
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Setting the PBKDF2 iteration parameter too low will result in significant reduction of the resulting hash's security. 
Modern hash functions usually have a cost (or similar) parameter the user can set to determine how much computational power should be used in hashing the password. A higher value means a slower computation, but also makes it slower to attack, as each attempt will take longer to perform. 

Cause

How does it happen

The iteration parameter for the PBKDF2 function is too low. 
Setting too low a cost value may significantly reduce the security of the password hash. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • PBKDF2's iteration parameter should be set at a minimum value of 10.000 or higher. Lowering this number will reduce the computational effort required for computing hash from the password, weakening the resulting hash, making it easier for an attacker to crack it. 
    • Choosing an appropriate cost parameter depends on the underlying hashing algorithm in place and what the purpose of the key derivation function is. The most common purpose is authenticating interactive logins, so the threshold values on the cost parameters for this query have been set accordingly. 

]]

rule.name: PBKDF2_Weak_Salt_Value
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Using a weak pseudo-random number generator's value or a static value for the PBKDF2 salt will result in significant reduction of the resulting hash's security. 

Cause

How does it happen

The salt parameter for the credential storage function is not secure. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Salts are used to prevent an attacker from creating a rainbow-table and performing a lookup of hashes instead of a brute-force attack on a user's password hash. Having a unique and unpredictable salt per password will also prevent attackers from knowing which users share the same password. Best practices include the use of a Cryptographically-Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator (CSPRNG) to get the salt value. 

]]

rule.name: Compromised_CDN
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Web content imported from a CDN serving malicious code can redirect web-pages, download malicious or unwanted files, or inject malicious code to affect or steal a user's session within the context of the application it is being used in. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application relies on data served by a CDN, which serves web-content and code that is embedded into the web-page. However this CDN has been compromised which means it should not be trusted. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Remove all uses of compromised CDNs 
    • Review all uses of software that was potentially obtained from the CDN and replace it with trusted, secure code 
    • Consider hosting all web-content on trusted repositories rather than relying on public 3rd party CDNs 

]]

rule.name: Cookie_Overly_Broad_Path
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Cookies often contain sensitive information, such as session tokens or CSRF tokens; failure to ensure their exposure is minimized to their intended scope of operations via a granular path may put its content at risk. 

Cause

How does it happen

Cookie configurations allow setting an intended path for cookies, which refer to which subdirectories within the application to whom a cookie should be served. Setting this path to "/" will allow any path within the application to read the contents of the cookie. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Review cookie configurations to ensure a sensitive cookie is only ever submitted under its intended path, unless otherwise required. 

]]

rule.name: Dangerous_File_Extension
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker that exploits this vulnerability could cause the application server to execute arbitrary code, allowing the attacker to alter the application, run any operating system command, and even take over the server altogether, depending on the application's system privileges. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application allows users to upload a file to the application, which is saved to a file within the website's directory. The application does not apply thorough validation checks on the uploaded file, especially with regard to the file type or contents. This enables the attacker to upload executable files, in particular web server code such as .ASP, .PHP, .JSP files, and others.  
When this is followed by a regular request to the web application for the previously uploaded files, the application server will then execute the code in the uploaded file, giving the attacker direct access to the command execution environment. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Storage: If possible, avoid saving uploaded files to disk on the server; instead storing them in external data storage, e.g., database or document management system. 
    • Location: User files should be stored in an isolated directory, outside of the web site's directory with direct browsing disabled. When required, the application should explicitly read the file in code and stream the contents to the user applicatively. 
    • Assurance of non-execution: Files uploaded from users should be explicitly marked as non-executable by the web / application server, e.g., in a configuration file or by directory. 
    • Validation: Always validate all user input. In particular, enforce an allow-list of allowed file types, according to the file extension and/or MIME type. Do not allow arbitrary files (such as .ASP, .PHP, .JSP, .EXE, .HTML, and so on). For example, accept only images such as .GIF, .JPG, .PNG, .BMP; these lists should be based on business requirements. If business requirements include non-media files such as documents, executables or code - consider adding another layer of security which would scan these files for malicious content. 
    • Renaming: Explicitly impose a pre-defined extension according to the file type before saving the file to disk. This can be a hardcoded extension or a configured list of allowed file types. 
    • Privileges: As a measure of Defense-in-Depth, configure the application server to execute in a limited system account with minimal OS privileges. 

]]

rule.name: Deprecated_Functions_Methods_or_Properties
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Using deprecated code in a code base means relying on code that has been declared unmaintained, for any number of reasons. Certain deprecations occur when code is not secure enough, while others may be completely unrelated to security. However - all code that is deprecated will not be maintained, which means that even if it is not known to be vulnerable at present, that may change - its status as deprecated will ensure that if a vulnerability is ever discovered it will likely never be reported or fixed. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses code that has been declared deprecated. It is likely that the code that references the obsolete element was developed before it was declared as obsolete, and in the meantime the referenced code was updated. 

]]

rule.name: Deprecated_Modules_Libraries_or_Packages
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Introducing deprecated code into a code base means relying on code that has been declared unmaintained, for any number of reasons. Certain deprecations occur when code is not secure enough, while others may be completely unrelated to security. However - all code that is deprecated will not be maintained, which means that even if it is not known to be vulnerable at present, that may change - its status as deprecated will ensure that if a vulnerability is ever discovered it will likely never be reported or fixed. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application relies on imported code that has been deprecated. It is likely that the imported code that references the deprecated element was developed before it was declared as obsolete, which would require working around it to exclude. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always prefer to use the most updated versions of libraries, packages, and other dependencies. 
    • Seek a secure, maintained alternative to the imported code. 
    • Do not use or reference any class, method, function, property, or other element that has been declared deprecated. 

]]

rule.name: Divide_By_Zero
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When a program divides a number by zero, an exception will be raised. If this exception is not handled by the application, unexpected results may occur, including crashing the application. This can be considered a DoS (Denial of Service) attack, if an external user has control of the value of the denominator or can cause this error to occur. 

Cause

How does it happen

The program receives an unexpected value, and uses it for division without filtering, validation, or verifying that the value is not zero. The application does not explicitly handle this error or prevent division by zero from occuring. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Before dividing by an unknown value, validate the number and explicitly ensure it does not evaluate to zero.  
    • Validate all untrusted input from all sources, in particular verifying that it is not zero before dividing with it.  
    • Verify output of methods, calculations, dictionary lookups, and so on, and ensure it is not zero before dividing with the result.  
    • Ensure divide-by-zero errors are caught and handled appropriately. 

]]

rule.name: Environment_Variable_Injection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Note that in Go setting environment variables from within code does so for the current process and any child processes - somewhat mitigating the risk of a system-wide effect from injecting environment variables. 
Environment variables are often trusted within the code-base as having arrived from within the system or set by local administrators. Additionally, environment variables are often utilized by external software and services. An attacker who can manipulate environment variables may use this trust to trigger arbitrary system commands, modify settings to suit their needs or simply break functionality. 

Cause

How does it happen

Potentially user-tainted values are set as environment variables by code. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Never store user-provided values directly inside environment variables - consider an alternative solution for storage. 

]]

rule.name: Heap_Inspection
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

All variables stored by the application in unencrypted memory can potentially be retrieved by an unauthorized user, with privileged access to the machine. For example, a privileged attacker could attach a debugger to the running process, or retrieve the process's memory from the swapfile or crash dump file. Once the attacker finds the user passwords in memory, these can be reused to easily impersonate the user to the system. 

Cause

How does it happen

String variables are immutable - in other words, once a string variable is assigned, its value cannot be changed or removed. Thus, these strings may remain around in memory, possibly in multiple locations, for an indefinite period of time until the garbage collector happens to remove it. Sensitive data, such as passwords, will remain exposed in memory as plaintext with no control over their lifetime. 
While it may still be possible to retrieve data from memory, even if it uses a mutable container that is cleared, or retrieve a decryption key and decrypt sensitive data from memory - layering sensitive data with these types of protection would significantly increase the required effort to do so. By setting a high bar for retrieving sensitive data from memory, and reducing the amount and exposure of sensitive data in memory, an adversary is significantly less likely to succeed in obtaining valuable data. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When it comes to avoiding Heap Inspection, it is important to note that, given any read access to memory or a memory dump of an application, it is always likely to disclose some sensitive data to an adversary - these suggestions are part of defense-in-depth principles for protection of sensitive data in cases where such memory read access is successfully obtained. These recommendations will enable significant reduction in the lifespan and exposure of sensitive data in memory; however - given enough time, effort and unlimited access to memory, they will only go so far in protecting sensitive data being used by the application. The only way to handle Heap Inspection issues is to minimize and reduce data exposure, and obscure it in memory wherever possible. 
    • Do not store sensitive data, such as passwords or encryption keys, in memory in plain-text, even for a short period of time.  
    • Prefer to use specialized classes that store encrypted data in memory to ensure it cannot be trivially retrieved from memory. 
    • When required to use sensitive data in its raw form, temporarily store it in mutable data types, such as byte arrays, to reduce readability from memory, and then promptly zeroize the memory locations, to reduce exposure duration of this data while in memory. 
    • Ensure that memory dumps are not exchanged with untrusted parties, as even by ensuring all of the above - it may still be possible to reverse-engineer encrypted containers, or retrieve bytes of sensitive data from memory and rebuild it. 

]]

rule.name: Improper_Error_Handling
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An unhandled error may cause unexpected behavior if it is not properly checked, depending on implementation the likeliest scenario being denial-of-service if the unhandled error aggregates, or triggers further errors downstream. A suppressed error or one that is not properly logged and documented will likely lead to loss of relevant information, hinder troubleshooting and potentially obscure code quality and security related issues. 

Cause

How does it happen

An error is thrown, but is not handled - the error itself is either intentionally suppressed or, through a certain logic flow, is never actively handled. If an error is properly suppressed or never used, it is implicitly suppressed - this implies it is not logged or logically validated by application code. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • In Go, when using panic() or a panic-prone piece of code (such as a 3rd party library), always consider the following: 
    • recover() must be deferred via the defer keyword - otherwise, the value of recover() would be nil, and then when the panic call occurs nothing will "catch" it 
    • A call to recover() must be immediately in the deferred function, which is either anonymous or named. If the deferred function calls another function that contains recover(), its value would be nil and the thrown panic will continue after deferred code has finished running 
    • Goroutines which panic cannot be recovered by their calling code. If a deferred recover() call precedes a call to panic-prone code that is invoked as a Go routine (via go), the deferred code will be ignored, panic will terminate the program and a stack trace for every ongoing routine will be dumped 
    • Return values from calls to recover() should be handled like errors - they should be logged, and should fit code flow in case a panic was caused 
    • Always log errors to ensure availability of error-related information 
    • Perform logical checks when handling error-prone code to root out any potential unexpected behavior in case an operation fails 
    • Cover all potential edge cases, however unlikely their occurrence may be, to avoid troubleshooting problems in the future 

]]

rule.name: Improper_Resource_Shutdown_or_Release
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Unreleased resources can cause a drain of those available for system use, eventually causing general reliability and availability problems, such as performance degradation, process bloat, and system instability. If a resource leak can be intentionally exploited by an attacker, it may be possible to cause a widespread DoS (Denial of Service) attack. This might even expose sensitive information between unprivileged users, if the resource continues to retain data or user id between subsequent allocations. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application code allocates resource objects, but does not ensure these are always closed and released in a timely manner. This can include database connections, file handles, network sockets, or any other resource that needs to be released. In some cases, these might be released - but only if everything works as planned; if there is any runtime exception during the normal course of system operations, resources start to leak.  
Note that even in managed-memory languages, certain resources must be explicitly released. Many types of resource are not released even when the Garbage Collector runs; and even if the the object would eventually release the resource, such an automatic release is often not controlled. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always close and release all resources that do not close when they are no longer in use. 
    • Ensure resources are released (along with any other necessary cleanup) in a deferred code block, such as finally, that always executes; alternatively ensure resources are closed at the end of logic that is not error-prone. Do not close resources while handling exceptions and errors, since there are no guarantees it will be called. 

]]

rule.name: Improper_Transaction_Handling
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Database transactions that are abandoned (if their associated connection is closed, before the transaction is committed or rolled back) can have several different results, depending on implementation and specific technologies in use. While in some scenarios the database will automatically roll back the transaction if the connection is closed, more often it will either automatically commit the transaction in its abortive state, or leave the transaction open indefinitely (depending on its configured timeout value).  
In the first case, a transaction that is committed after a runtime exception is likely to be in an inconsistent state, incompatible with the current runtime conditions. This would result in situation detrimental to the system's integrity and possibly even stability.  
In the second case, a transaction that is kept active indefinitely would cause the database server to retain its locks on all records and tables affected by the transaction. This could cause general reliability and availability problems, leading to delays, degraded performance, or even deadlocks as one thread waits for the locks to be released.  
In either case this results in unexpected state, and is dependent on external factors such that the application is not controlling the result. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application creates a connection to the database, and explicitly manages the database transaction by committing it when appropriate. However, the code does not explicitly roll back failed transactions, for example in the case of exceptions. This causes the application to rely on implementation-specific behavior, depending on the specific combination of technologies (such as the database server) and resultant configuration. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always open database connections and begin transactions within a try { } block.  
    • Ensure there are no active uncommitted transactions before closing a database connection.  
    • Always rollback active transactions in the case of exceptions. 
    • After handling the exception, ensure the transaction is rolled back in the catch { } block, or possibly in the finally { } block. 

]]

rule.name: Incorrect_Permission_Assignment_For_File_System_Resources
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Exposing files and directories to unintended users could allow them to read, modify or even execute files. 

Cause

How does it happen

In Go, the default permissions set when creating a file without setting its permissions is 666 - which would expose the contents of the file to other OS users for both reading and writing. 
A file system resource is created without setting explicit access permissions. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always apply the Principle of Least Privilege to all files and directories - restrict access to the bare minimum required 
    • Even if the default behavior provides the required privilege, it is always recommended to set the required permissions explicitly to ensure portability and coherent secure design 

]]

rule.name: Incorrect_Reflect_Value_Comparison
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Incorrectly comparing 2 interfaces may affect security or functionality related decisions, and whose impact will vary based on implementation. The most likely scenario, however, is stability issues due to unexpected application behavior. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application compares 2 different reflected interfaces based on their interface value (i.e. reflect.ValueOf( i )) rather than the underlying value (i.e. reflect.ValueOf( i ).Interface()). 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • To properly compare 2 different reflected interfaces, make sure you always call the Interface() method to retrieve the underlying value of the interface (even when the method reflect.DeepEqual(interface1, interface2) is used to compare the interfaces). 

]]

rule.name: Insufficient_Session_Expiration
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Insufficient session expiration increases the exposure for attackers to execute session hijacking attacks, which will allow attackers to reuse a valid session and impersonate an authenticated user in the application. 

Cause

How does it happen

An active session that does not properly expire will remain in the system for a prolonged amount of time, if not indefinitely, which could unneccessarily increase its exposure in the long run. This exposure could allow attackers the opportunity to obtain these session tokens, and impersonate authenticated users. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always set a reasonable idle session timeout, depending on the application's requirement - for most applications this is around 15-30 minutes, and never more than 24 hours (86400 seconds). 
    • Make sure that all sessions timeout eventually. Refine and fine-tune session expiration to the minimal value for a session timeout. 

]]

rule.name: Integer_Overflow
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An arithmetic overflow will lead to undefined behavior and unintentional effects, such as data corruption (e.g. value wraparound, wherein maximum values become minimum values); system crashes; infinite loops; logic errors, such as bypassing of security mechanisms; truncation or loss of data; or even buffer overflows leading to arbitrary code execution, when performing memory operations with an overflowed numeric value. 

Cause

How does it happen

All numeric data-types have a bit-wise representation. If, after an arithmetic operation, a value exceeds its bit-wise representation's amount of bits, then the most significant numbers that are being added will simply be truncated, with the value that remains after this truncation being the leftover from the wraparound action - this is known as an "Arithmetic Overflow", or its common misnomer - "Integer Overflow", which is misleading, since this applies to many other types. If data-types that can overflow drop below their minimum value, they will wraparound negatively in what is commonly referred to as an underflow. 
For example, if an unsigned 32bit integer is set to 4,294,967,295 and 1 is added, it will overflow and wraparound to 0. If it were a signed 32bit integer with the value 2,147,483,647 and 1 is added, it will overflow and wraparound to -2,147,483,648. 
To ensure code correctness, checks must be made that values are within expected bounds so that the result of arithmetic operations will not overflow or underflow. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When performing arithmetic operations on data that may contain any value, consider adding a check to ensure that this data is within bounds where the product of those operations would not result in an overflow nor an underflow. 
    • Consider creating wrappers for all arithmetic operations that would have specific handling for exceptional conditions; for example, by throwing an exception if checks show an overflow had or would have occurred. 

]]
